title: Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations
lead: The tangent plane to a surface plays the part the tangent line played for a curve. This section finds its equation from the partial derivatives, uses it as a linear approximation, defines when a function of two or three variables is differentiable, and estimates changes and errors with the total differential.
objectives: Determine the equation of a plane tangent to a given surface at a point.
Use the tangent plane to approximate a function of two variables at a point.
Explain when a function of two variables is differentiable.
Use the total differential to approximate the change in a function of two variables.
summary_html:
• The analog of a tangent line to a curve is a tangent plane to a surface for functions of two variables.
  • Tangent planes can be used to approximate values of functions near known values.
  • A function is differentiable at a point if it is ”smooth” at that point (i.e., no corners or discontinuities exist at that point).
  • The total differential can be used to approximate the change in a function $z=\kf(x_{0},y_{0})$ at the point $(x_{0},y_{0})$ for given values of $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y.$

For the following exercises, use the figure shown here.

The length of line segment $BC$ is equal to what mathematical expression?

For the following exercises, use the figure shown here.

Using the figure, explain what the length of line segment $AB$ represents.

answer.solution: In the figure, $C$ is level with $(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}),$ $B$ is on the tangent plane and $A$ on the surface, all above $(x_{0}+\Delta x,y_{0}+\Delta y).$ So $AC$ is the actual change $\Delta z=f(x_{0}+\Delta x,y_{0}+\Delta y)-f(x_{0},y_{0}),$ $BC$ is the differential $dz=f_{x}(x_{0},y_{0})\Delta x+f_{y}(x_{0},y_{0})\Delta y,$ and $AB=\Delta z-dz$ is the error of the linear approximation: how far the surface lies from its tangent plane there. For a differentiable function this error shrinks faster than the distance $\sqrt{(\Delta x)^{2}+(\Delta y)^{2}}.$

exercises.prompt: Show that $f(x,y)=e^{xy}x$ is differentiable at point $(1,0).$

answer.solution: Using the definition of differentiability, we have $e^{xy}x\approx x+y.$

exercises.prompt: Show that $f(x,y)=x^{2}+3y$ is differentiable at every point. In other words, show that $\Delta z=f(x+\Delta x,y+\Delta y)-f(x,y)=f_{x}\Delta x+f_{y}\Delta y+{ε}_{1}\Delta x+{ε}_{2}\Delta y,$ where both ${ε}_{1}$ and ${ε}_{2}$ approach zero as $(\Delta x,\Delta y)$ approaches $(0,0).$

answer.solution: $\Delta z=2x\Delta x+3\Delta y+{(\Delta x)}^{2}.$ ${(\Delta x)}^{2}\to 0$ for small $\Delta x$ and $z$ satisfies the definition of differentiability.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, determine whether the statement is true or false. Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The linear approximation to the function of $f(x,y)=5x^{2}+x\;\tan (y)$ at $(2,\pi )$ is given by $L(x,y)=22+21(x-2)+(y-\pi ).$

answer.solution: False. At $(2,\pi ),$ $f(2,\pi )=5(4)+2\tan \pi =20,$ $f_{x}=10x+\tan y=20$ and $f_{y}=x\sec^{2}y=2.$ The linear approximation is $L(x,y)=20+20(x-2)+2(y-\pi ),$ not $22+21(x-2)+(y-\pi ).$
